# Issue #642: The prover follows a `let mut` through each assignment (ADR-361 D9)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/642).

`ready` · opened 2026-10-17 · updated 2026-10-17 · 1 comment

## How it came up

For the owner's loop program (#640), the prover had to read `let mut i = 0` and `let mut total = 0`, or it would not know the loop's start. Commit 8bfd1a0 made a `let mut` a name of the prover **until its first assignment** (where no call is handed it and no lambda changes it); after an assignment outside a loop, it forgets it. Part III 14.2 and ADR-269 D9 said only "bindings that do not change", so the build went past the text.

```nika
let mut x = 0
assert(x == 0)   // proved today: x has not changed yet
x = x + 1
assert(x == 1)   // checked at run time today; proved after this issue
```

## Decision (owner, 2026-10-17)

Option B: follow every assignment, the static single assignment form Dafny, SPARK, CBMC and Kani use. Before the first assignment no SSA is needed: the binding has not changed (as built). Rejected: knowing a `let mut` only until its first assignment.

* Why: [ADR-361 D9](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-361.md); ADR-269 D9 notes the change.
* What: Part III 14.2, *What the prover reads*.

## To build

1. An assignment `x = e` to a tracked `let mut` (no call handed it, no lambda or deferred body changes it) gives `x` a new name with `e`'s value over the old one; compound assignments (`+=`, `-=`, `*=` by a constant) likewise. Test: `x = x + 1; assert(x == 1)` proved; `x = x * 3; assert(x == 3)` after `x = 1` proved.
2. After an `if`/`else` that changes `x` on one side or both, `x` is either side's value with that side's condition (a disjunction over the branch condition), and an `if` without `else` keeps the old value on the other side. Test: `if c { x = 1 } else { x = 2 }; assert(x >= 1 && x <= 2)` proved; `assert(x == 1)` not proved.
3. A `match` arm that changes `x` forgets it after the `match` (as today), unless the arms are read; not required here. A loop keeps reading through its invariant (#640).
4. A binding handed to a call (`f(ref mut x)` or any `mut` parameter) or changed from a lambda stays out, from its `let` on. Test: such an `x` after `x = 1` gives no fact; never a false proof.
5. A claim decided without the new names never pays: second query only for a claim left open (ADR-361 D2). Counters: `NIKAIA_PROVER_COUNTS` before/after on the standalone files and `lower-std`; callgrind ≤ +5 %.
6. Refutations: a claim the assignments make false is `NK1207` only under ADR-269's rule for what reaches; check every new `NK1207` in the corpus by hand.

Related: #640 (loops), ADR-269 D9, D16.

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-10-17](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/642#issuecomment-6241418410)

Steps 1-2 built in 4cc925d (0.0.1009): an assignment (`=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=` by a constant) and an `if`/`else` are followed with SSA names (`x#<byte>`); an old value known to be a number is substituted, so a loop after it still knows its start. The new facts are asked only for a claim still open (a second query), and used for refutation and a loop's entry. The owner's program's prover counters are unchanged. Tests: `crates/nikaia/tests/prove_mutables.rs` (8).

Still open:
* preconditions and index bounds at a call read only the ordinary facts, not the history;
* a loop after `x` was assigned from another variable (not a known number) finds no invariant;
* steps 3-6 of the list (match arms, the measurement, refutations checked by hand).

# Issue #643: `[v; n]`: a list or an array of n copies of a value that copies (ADR-362 D1-D4)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/643).

`ready` · opened 2026-10-17 · updated 2026-10-17 · 0 comments

## How it came up

The owner wrote `let safety_buffer = [0..181]` for 181 numbers (the loop program of #640). That is a list of one range; printing an element is `NK1201` (#638), indexing it with 110 aborts. Asking how to write 181 equal elements without a loop showed a gap, checked with the compiler on 2026-10-17:

| Written | Today |
| :--- | :--- |
| `(0..<181).map(fn(_i) { 0 }).collect()` | `Vec` of 181 zeros |
| `let mut xs = []` then `xs.resize(181, 0)` | `Vec` of 181 zeros (lowered to `vec[0; 181]`, solver-workload §8.1) |
| `let xs: Array[i64, 181] = (0..<181).collect()` | `NK1103` |
| `[0; 181]` | syntax error *Expected `]` here, but found `;`* |

An `Array[T, N]` of more than a handful of elements cannot be written at all, though ADR-152 made it the container without allocation.

## Decision (owner, 2026-10-17)

* Spelling `[v; n]` (Rust's); rejected: a function `repeat(v, n)`, `[v] * n`, `[v ** n]`, nothing.
* A value that does not copy is **refused** (`NK1280`), not cloned.
* Why: [ADR-362](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-362.md). What: Part I 4.5 (lists, `Array[T, N]`), Part III's table (`NK1157`, `NK1280`).

## To build

1. Parser: `[expr; expr]` as a list literal of its own kind (no other `;` inside brackets). Test: `[0; 3]`, `[x + 1; n]`, nested `[[0; 2]; 3]`; `[1, 2; 3]` is a syntax error.
2. Checker: the type from the use as every list literal (ADR-152 D4) — no use: `Vec[T]`; `Array[T, N]` wanted: `n` must be a `comptime` integer equal to `N`, else `NK1157` naming both (also for an `n` the build does not know). For a `Vec`, `n` is any whole number type. Tests: `let b: Array[u8, 4096] = [0; 4096]` builds; `[0; 4095]` there is `NK1157`; `let v = [0; n]` with a parameter `n` is a `Vec[i64]`.
3. `NK1280`: `v` not a value that copies (`String`, `Vec`, a struct owning one); the help writes `(0..<n).map(fn(_i) { v.clone() }).collect()`. Test: `[name; 3]` with `name: String` refused with the help; `[(1, 2); 3]` and `[Point { x: 0, y: 0 }; 3]` (a value struct of numbers) build.
4. Lowering: `vec[v; n as usize]` for a `Vec` (a negative `n` aborts as an index out of range does, ADR-293: check before the cast), `[v; N]` for an array. Test: the output of a program printing `len()` and elements; a negative length aborts with the index message.
5. Prover: `len()` of `[v; n]` is `n` (and `N` for an array). Test: `let xs = [0; 181]; assert(xs.len() == 181)` proved; an index `b` with `0 <= b && b < 181` known needs no check.
6. `tools/*.nika`: replace the `resize` workarounds where one builds a list of equal values, if any (`grep -n 'resize('`); not required.

The owner's program then writes `let safety_buffer = [0; 181]`.

Related: #640, #638; the warning for `[0..181]` (ADR-362 D5) is its own issue.

# Issue #649: Standard input and files are untrusted unless marked `trusted: true` (ADR-365)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/649).

`compiler`, `ready` · opened 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18 · 0 comments

## How it came up

The owner asked what happens to an `assert` on input data (stdin, sockets, files). Tried with the binary of 2026-10-17:

* `let n = text::parse_i64(io::read_to_string().trim()) ?? 0` then `assert(n > 0)` builds; with input `0` the program stops with exit 101 (*assertion failed, n is 0*).
* The same claim about `process::run`'s output (and a socket) is refused: `NK1202` *a claim about data from outside the program*, with a guard as help (test `data_from_outside_is_checked_by_a_guard_and_not_asserted` in `prove.rs`).
* The difference is `provenance` in `std.contracts`: `io::read`, `io::lines`, `io::read_to_string`, `fs::read`, `fs::read_to_string`, `fs::map`, `fs::walk`, `cli::args` are `trusted` (ADR-010 D2: the operator chose the bytes); only `process::run` and `net::Connection::read` are `untrusted`.
* ADR-010 D3's marker at the source, `fs::map(path; trusted: false)`, is not built: `NK1109`, *has no option called `trusted`*.

The owner wants `NK1202` for stdin and for files nobody vouches for.

## Decision (2026-10-18, owner: option B)

[ADR-365](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-365.md): standard input and every file read while the program runs are **untrusted**; a source marked `trusted: true` is trusted; the project's own assets (`asset("…")`, read while building) are trusted without a marker. ADR-010 D2/D3 changed (*Changed by* notes), Part III 14.2 and 17.1. Rejected: keep both trusted with `trusted: false` (fails open), stdin untrusted and files trusted (a path does not say who wrote the file). Not decided: `cli::args` and the environment (trusted as before; `main`'s parameters are checked by ADR-360).

Consequence the owner accepted: maps keyed by file data get the keyed hash unless the read says `trusted: true`; `benches/brc` writes the marker where needed.

## To build

1. **The `trusted:` option** on every source in `std.contracts` (`io::read`, `io::read_to_string`, `io::lines`, the `fs` reads, `fs::map`, `fs::walk`, `fs::read_dir`; and `trusted: false`/`true` on the untrusted ones as ADR-010 D3 has it), recorded in the ledger with its place. Test: `fs::read_to_string(p, fs::Root::Anywhere; trusted: true)` builds; an unknown value is refused.
2. **The default:** `provenance = "untrusted"` for those entries. Tests: `assert` on stdin data is `NK1202` with the guard help; after `throw … if !(…)` it is proved; with `trusted: true` it is a runtime check again.
3. **The hasher:** a map keyed by file data is keyed unless `trusted: true`; `--trust` prints the marker's place (Part III 17.1's example). Test with `--trust` output.
4. **Programs in the repository:** `benches/brc` (and any bench that reads its own fixture) gets `trusted: true`; rerun `benches/brc/brc.sh` and confirm the instruction count is unchanged; `examples/` and `tools/*.nika` that now meet `NK1202` or a keyed hash get the marker where they read their own data (the toolchain reads source files the user wrote: trusted is right there).
5. Test blocks that read the package's fixtures: decide in the build whether `test` reads are trusted (they read what the package holds) and note it here if it needs the owner.

Related: #579 (the question came from the converter round), ADR-010, ADR-269 D6.

# Issue #654: ref String: build the NK1261 warning, close the `ref int` gap in NK1257, migrate, then refuse

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/654).

`ready` · opened 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-19 · 7 comments

The owner asked whether `ref` is still used without a warning. Checked against today's compiler (727bb97):

**What is decided**
- ADR-282 D2 and Part III: `ref String` outside `extern "C"` / `pub extern fn` is warning `NK1261` (*`ref` is redundant here, the ledger records it*). It becomes a refusal once the specification, `examples/` and `tools/*.nika` carry none.
- ADR-354 D2: `ref` on a word (a number, `bool`, `scalar`, a data-less enum) is refusal `NK1257` at every position.
- `ref T` on other types (structs, `Vec`, `Expr`) stays the written assertion of a view (ADR-184 D1). It is not part of this issue.

**What the compiler does**
1. `NK1261` is **not built**: `fn s(t: ref String)` passes `nikaia check`, `run` and `build` without any warning. No code mentions `NK1261`.
2. `NK1257` misses the `int` alias: `fn s(t: ref int)` passes silently, while `fn s(t: ref i64)` is refused.
3. Count of `ref String`, still written:

   | Where | Count |
   | :--- | ---: |
   | `tools/*.nika` | 1961 |
   | `examples/` | 289 |
   | `crates/rs2nika/convert/src` | 136 (and the converter writes `ref String` for `&str` into its drafts) |
   | Part I, Part II, Part III | 36, 6, 19 |
   | `benches/` | 8 |
   | `scripts/` | 2 |

# Issue #658: The fast `nikaia run` path ignores RUSTFLAGS, the Cargo path honours it

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/658).

`decision` · opened 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18 · 0 comments

Found by the #653 round (cafe1d8).

Since 0.0.1016 `nikaia run` calls rustc directly against a std dylib (`run_fast.rs`) when a program needs no Cargo dependency, and goes through Cargo otherwise. Cargo passes `RUSTFLAGS` on to rustc; the fast path does not. So `RUSTFLAGS="-D warnings" nikaia run p.nika` denies warnings or not depending on whether the program has a dependency. The backend-error tests now point `RUSTC` at a wrapper instead, which works on both paths.

CLAUDE.md's measuring rules use `RUSTFLAGS="-C overflow-checks=off"` for a second row; that row is measured through `nikaia build`, but the same mismatch would hit anyone using `run` for it.

## Question for the owner
Should the fast path honour `RUSTFLAGS` like Cargo (append it to its rustc line), or is `RUSTFLAGS` not part of `nikaia run`'s contract at all (then Part III says so and the Cargo path stops passing it)?

Recommendation: honour it — `nikaia run` should not change meaning with a program's dependencies, and Cargo's behaviour is what users of Rust tooling expect.

## To build (once decided)
1. Per the answer, the fast path appends `RUSTFLAGS` (split as Cargo does) to its rustc invocation, or both paths ignore it.
2. Test: a program with an unused variable under `RUSTFLAGS="-D warnings"` gives the same verdict on both paths.

# Issue #659: Decision: is a text position that only literals fill a view of static text, or text of its own?

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/659).

`ready` · opened 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-19 · 3 comments

## What this is about

A text literal like `"Hamburg"` is part of the compiled program: the bytes already sit in the binary, for as long as the program runs. Where a program only *reads* a literal (`println("Hamburg")`, `greet("Ada")`), nothing is allocated. The question is what happens where a literal is **stored** — in a struct field, as a function's result, in a list — and nothing but literals is ever stored there.

```nikaia
pub struct Row {
    name: String,
    note: String,
}

fn main() {
    let mut rows = Vec()
    for i in 0..<n {
        rows.push(Row { name: "Hamburg", note: "a note with <angles>" })
    }
    ...
}
```

Today every `Row` gets two fresh heap copies of text the binary already holds:

```rust
pub struct Row { name: String, note: String }
rows.push(Row { name: String::from("Hamburg"), note: String::from("a note with <angles>") });
```

With `ref String` written on the fields (as `benches/template.nika` does today), the same program lowers to views of the static text and copies nothing:

```rust
pub struct Row<'a, 'a1> { name: &'a str, note: &'a1 str }
rows.push(Row { name: "Hamburg", note: "a note with <angles>" });
```

## Where the question comes from

#654 (ADR-282 D2: `String` is a view wherever a view suffices, so `ref String` is to go away) needs every `ref String` in our programs to be droppable without changing the lowering. The #654 builder (0.0.1022) found that this one position does change: `benches/template.nika`'s `Row` gets copies when `ref` is dropped. It is the only remaining class besides option defaults (#654 step 0 c1, being built). Nothing breaks either way — it is a cost question, and a question of what the language promises about literals. It needs an answer before NK1261 turns `ref String` into a refusal (#654 step 6), because after that a program has no way to ask for the view.

## What is decided today

- **Part I 2.3 (the specification) decides it: copies.** "where the use **keeps** it — a field, an annotated `let`, a `return`, an argument the callee keeps — it is constructed there, as `[1, 2]` is a `Vec` where one is wanted". ADR-282 D3/D4 say the same, and D17 for a `let` and an all-literal `if`/`match`.
- **ADR-282 D13 contradicts itself on it.** Its table counts "literals as views of static text", so a position only literals flow into would be *views only* → a view. The sentence under it says "A literal alone moves nothing: a position only literals and text of its own flow into stays `String`" — which covers literals *mixed with* text of its own, not literals alone. Whichever way this is decided, D13 is to be reworded.
- The compiler follows Part I. Checked on 0.0.1022:

| what is stored | lowered today |
| :--- | :--- |
| a field filled only by literals | `String::from("…")` |
| a result `if big { "large" } else { "small" }` | `String::from` in each branch |
| `Team { names: ["Ada", "Grace"] }` into `Vec[String]` | `vec[String::from(…), …]` |
| a local `Vec` filled by `push("Ada")`, then put in a `Vec[String]` field | **refused, NK1106** — contradicts D16 ("a list that already has a position is linked to where it goes"); a defect whichever option is chosen |

## Measured

`benches/template.nika` (n rows through `dsl html`), both variants lowered by today's compiler, `rustc -C opt-level=3`, no LTO, against the release `nikaia_std`; same output byte for byte. callgrind `--branch-sim=yes`:

| rows | view (`&str`) | copy (`String`) | copy / view |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2 000 | 2 891 572 instr., 30 642 mispredicts | 4 589 236 instr., 37 256 mispredicts | 1.59× |
| 20 000 | 23 550 344 instr., 228 721 mispredicts | 41 035 481 instr., 289 312 mispredicts | 1.74× |

That is **≈ 874 instructions per row, ≈ 437 per stored literal** (an allocation, a copy, a free) — in a benchmark that also escapes and renders HTML for every row. Overflow checks on in both.

## How others do it

Go, Java, Swift, Python and JavaScript store a literal without copying it: the string value points at the static bytes (Java and Python intern them, Swift marks them immortal, Go's string header points into read-only data). Rust makes the programmer choose (`&'static str`, `String`, or `Cow<'static, str>`). C++'s `std::string` copies (small strings inline), `std::string_view` does not. A script-like language whose literal costs an allocation the moment it is stored is the exception.

## Options

**A — keep it: a stored literal is text of its own** (Part I 2.3 as it stands).
Every literal kept in a field, result or list is allocated, once per evaluation. Nothing changes in the specification; D13's sentence is reworded to say so. `benches/template` and every similar program pay ≈ 437 instructions per stored literal, and after NK1261 there is no way to avoid it.

**B — a position only literals flow into is a view of static text** (D13's table as written).
Below it is `&'static str` — no lifetime parameter, since static text outlives everything. As soon as text of its own also flows in, the position is mixed (`EitherText`, D14) or owned, as today. Part I 2.3's "constructed there" applies only where text of its own also flows in; D3, D4, D13, D17 are reworded. Risk: for a **published** struct, field or result, the representation depends on what the package itself puts there. A library whose `pub struct` is filled only with literals publishes a view of static text; a caller outside the package that wants to put its own `f"…"` there is refused (NK1106) until the library changes, which is a ledger diff (ADR-282 D2) — the same as for every other view today, but a new kind of surprise for a literal.

**C — B inside a package, `EitherText` at a published position.**
Unpublished positions as in B. A published position only literals flow into is mixed (`Cow<'static, str>` below): no allocation, any caller may store its own text, one branch per read. Costs a second rule and a branch on every read of such a field.

In every option, the NK1106 on a pushed-to local list (table above) is a defect and is fixed.

## Recommendation

**B.** It makes "a literal is a view of static text" (Part I 2.5, 2.4's example) true wherever the literal goes instead of only where it is read, it is what D13's table already says, it removes ≈ 437 instructions per stored literal, and it is what every comparable language does. The published-position risk is the general rule for views (ADR-282 D2, NK1106), and the ledger shows the change in review; if that proves to bite real libraries, C can be added later without changing any unpublished position.

## To build (once decided — written for B)
1. Spec: Part I 2.3 — a literal is constructed where it is kept *and text of its own also flows there*; a position only literals flow into holds a view of static text. ADR-282: reword D3, D4, D13 (the "literal alone" sentence), D17; a new D stating the decision and why A and C were rejected.
2. The tier walk counts a literal as a view of static text; a position with only such views lowers to `&'static str` (no lifetime parameter). Test: `benches/template.nika` with `ref` dropped lowers byte-identical except `&'static str` for the generic lifetimes; the all-literal result and the list literal above lower without `String::from`.
3. A local list linked to a field (D16) takes the field's tier; the pushed-to `Vec` above compiles. Test: that probe, and the same with one `f"…"` pushed (mixed).
4. Ledgers of examples and `tools/*.nika` regenerated; each change looked at.
5. `crates/nikaia/tests/measure.rs` gets the A/B above as a measurement.

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-10-18](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/659#issuecomment-6247609663)

**Decided by the owner: option B.** A literal is a view of the program's own text wherever it goes, not only where it is read.

- Why: [ADR-282 D29](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-282.md) (with the measurement and why A and C were rejected); D4, D13 and §5 reworded to match.
- What: Part I 2.2 (Text) and 2.3 (literals) — a position only literals and other views flow into holds the view; a literal is constructed only where text of its own also flows in.
- 0.0.1024 (766e817), specification only; the compiler follows with the list below.

#### To build
1. The tier walk counts a literal as a view of static text; a position into which only literals (and other views) flow lowers to `&'static str` (no lifetime parameter): a field, a result (also an all-literal `if`/`match`), a `let`, a list element, a map key or value. Test: `benches/template.nika` with `ref` dropped from `Row` lowers without `String::from` and with `&'static str` fields; `fn label(big: bool) -> String { if big { "large" } else { "small" } }` and `Team { names: ["Ada", "Grace"] }` lower without `String::from`; with one `f"…"` beside the literals, the literals are constructed as today.
2. A published position only literals flow into is a view in the ledger (D22); with text of its own also flowing in, it stays text of its own and the literals are constructed. Test: one of each, ledger lines checked.
3. A local list linked to a field (D16) takes the field's tier: `let mut names = Vec(); names.push("Ada"); Team { names: names }` compiles (no NK1106). Test: that probe; the same with an `f"…"` pushed.
4. `benches/template.nika` drops its `ref String`; ledgers of examples and `tools/*.nika` regenerated and each change looked at; `lower-std` diff committed.
5. `crates/nikaia/tests/measure.rs` gets the A/B of the issue body as a measurement.
6. The specification's own examples still pass (`--test specification`; regenerate `tests/specification/EXPECTED.txt` / `COMPILES.txt` only for what this changes).

Steps 1 and 3 built in 9b428ef, version 0.0.1036 (7623620).

- A field, a result (also an all-literal `if`/`match`), a `let`, a parameter or a list element into which only literals flow is a fourth tier (`Tier::Lasting`) and lowers to `&'static str`: no `String::from`, no lifetime parameter. `benches/template.nika` without `ref` lowers with no copy per row. # Issue #660: Decision: a `target-cpu` key, so a build can use the instructions of the machine it runs on

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/660).

`decision` · opened 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18 · 0 comments

## What this is about

A compiled program is machine code for a processor *family*: `x86_64-linux` code by default runs on every 64-bit x86 processor since 2003, so it may only use the instructions all of them have. Newer processors have wider vector instructions (AVX2, AVX-512 on x86; SVE on some ARM), `popcnt`, `lzcnt`, `bmi2` and more. A compiler told the exact processor ("`target-cpu`") may use them: a loop over bytes can handle 32 at a time instead of 16, a bit count is one instruction instead of a dozen.

```toml
[build.x86_64-linux]
opt-level = 3
target-cpu = "native"     # proposed: use everything the build machine has
```

## Where the question comes from

The owner asked for the website to say that Nikaia is fast and hardware-optimised (facec91 rewrote the lead). Today it can honestly say *optimised native machine code*, not *tuned to your processor*: no build sets a `target-cpu`. `crates/nikaia/src/sysroot.rs` (`Codegen`) already names `target-cpu` as "the obvious next" key of `[build.<target>]` and makes any such key a dimension of the compiled `std`'s cache key by construction (ADR-021 D13's obligation).

## Today

- Part III 13.3: `[build.<target>]` holds `opt-level`, `lto`, `incremental`, `debug`; a key it does not know fails the build. The table becomes the generated `Cargo.toml`'s profile.
- No `-C target-cpu` is passed anywhere (`nikaia build`, the fast `nikaia run` path of 0.0.1016, or the compiled `std`). Every binary is baseline `x86-64` / `aarch64` (generic).
- Benchmarks (`benches/brc`, `crates/nikaia/tests/measure.rs`) compare against Rust built the same way, so they are fair either way.

## What goes wrong if this is decided badly

- A binary built with `target-cpu = "native"` on a new machine and run on an older one **dies with an illegal-instruction signal** at the first unsupported instruction. No wrong value, but a crash with no message a user understands. This is the main argument against making `native` the default.
- `std` is compiled once per machine and cached (Part III 13.1); each distinct `target-cpu` is one more cached `std` (at most eight entries per kind are kept).
- Counts move: a benchmark built for `native` retires fewer, wider instructions. A table must say which CPU level it was counted at, or it compares unlike things.

## How others do it

- **Rust/Cargo, Clang, GCC**: baseline by default; `-C target-cpu=native` / `-march=native` opt-in; named levels `x86-64-v2`, `x86-64-v3` (AVX2), `x86-64-v4` (AVX-512) for a portable-but-newer binary.
- **Go**: `GOAMD64=v1..v4`, `v1` by default.
- **Zig**: `zig build` defaults to **native** for a build for the host, baseline for a cross build.
- **Java/.NET JIT**: always use the running CPU, since they compile on the machine that runs the code.
- **Function multiversioning** (GCC `target_clones`, Rust's `is_x86_feature_detected!`): one binary with several variants of a hot function, chosen at start. A library technique, not a build key.

## Options

**A — a `target-cpu` key in `[build.<target>]`, absent = baseline.** Values as rustc spells them (`native`, `x86-64-v3`, `neoverse-n1`, …). Portable by default, opt-in speed; same as Rust, Go, C. `nikaia build --target-cpu` overrides it for one build, as `--target` does.

**B — A, and absent = `native` for a build for the host machine** (Zig's choice), baseline for a cross build (`--target` differs from the host). The fastest program for someone who builds and runs on one machine, which is the script-like use the language aims at; a program copied to an older machine crashes.

**C — A, and `nikaia run` uses `native`** (it builds and runs on the same machine by definition, so it cannot hit the crash), while `nikaia build` stays baseline unless the key says otherwise.

## Measurements owed before deciding

1. `benches/brc` (`1brc.nika` against `tuned.rs`, both at the same level) at baseline, `x86-64-v3` and `native`: instructions and mispredicts per row, the same output byte for byte.
2. `crates/nikaia/tests/measure.rs`'s template and sparse-row workloads at baseline and `x86-64-v3`.
3. Whether the cached `std` built with `native` differs per machine in a way the cache key must capture (it should key on the resolved CPU name, not the word `native`).

## Recommendation

**C**: it gives `nikaia run` the full machine with no risk, keeps a built binary portable like every ahead-of-time toolchain except Zig, and the key (A) lets a deployment that knows its machines opt in. B's crash on another machine is a bad first experience for exactly the user the language invites.

## To build (written for C; adjusted once decided)
1. Part III 13.3: `target-cpu` in `[build.<target>]`, its values, absent = baseline for `nikaia build`, the machine's own CPU for `nikaia run`; `--target-cpu` on `build`. ADR: a new record or a D of ADR-002/ADR-037, with the options above.
2. `sysroot::Codegen` carries it; `native` is resolved to the CPU name (`rustc --print target-cpus` / `-C target-cpu=native` resolution) before it enters the cache key. Test: two builds with different values get two `std` entries; `native` on one machine reuses one entry.
3. The generated `Cargo.toml` / `RUSTFLAGS` path and the fast-run rustc line both pass `-C target-cpu`. Test: `nikaia run` of a probe whose lowered binary uses `popcnt` for `count_ones` on a machine that has it (check the disassembly), and a `nikaia build` binary without the key does not.
4. The measurements above in `benches/brc/README.md` and `measure.rs`, each row naming its CPU level.
5. The website may then say *tuned to your processor* for `nikaia run` and for a build that asks for it.

# Issue #664: 1BRC to the limit: no whole-file UTF-8 check, text checked only where it is new (measure first, incl. a type for unchecked text)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/664).

`libraries`, `compiler`, `performance`, `decision` · opened 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18 · 1 comment

Split from #422 (owner, 2026-10-18). #422 now only lets a grammar read `Bytes` ([ADR-366](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-366.md)); everything about speed is here, and is to be pushed as far as it goes.

## From zero

```nika
let data = fs::map(path, fs::Root::Anywhere)   // maps the file and checks all of it as UTF-8
let totals = Measurements::file(data)          // the grammar sees text
```

`fs::map` checks the whole mapping in one SIMD pass (`checked_text`, ADR-016 D1, D4), before the parse, so every `ref String` a grammar cuts from it is a view of the pages. A bad byte is `IoError::NotText("… (at byte N)")` before the first rule runs. `tuned` (Rust) checks nothing and turns only the 413 distinct names into text at the end - and reads a stray byte in a temperature as a wrong number.

ADR-016 §4 deferred *"fuse the check into the piece"*. ADR-366 now gives a grammar `Bytes` input with a check where text is made, so the shapes below can be built and measured.

## What is known

* Today (Nikaia 0.0.970, `benches/brc/README.md`, 1 M rows): **300.2** instructions a row; callgrind attributes **2.4** directly to `simdutf8`, plus an unsplit part of the 43.3 in "the rest, SIMD intrinsics". #422's "about 10" is from 0.0.424 and stale.
* **Not known, and it decides everything:** whether checking each name separately (9-16 bytes a row, std's short-input `from_utf8`) is cheaper than the whole-file SIMD pass. It may well be dearer. The only shape sure to be cheaper checks **a name only when it is new**: 413 checks instead of a billion. winnow-grammar does that for `intern` (its ADR 25 D4); Nikaia's 1BRC does not intern, the name goes as `ref String` into a `HashMap`'s `entry`.

## Shapes to measure

Each against today, same output byte for byte first, callgrind `--branch-sim=yes`, release, counts only (CLAUDE.md). Prototypes may be hand-edited generated Rust where the compiler cannot write them yet.

1. **Per-name check.** The grammar over the mapping's bytes (ADR-366), `NAME`'s `until` checked per row, no whole-file pass.
2. **Check on a miss, through the map.** The name stays bytes until the map lookup; a hit compares bytes against a key that is already text, so it needs no check; only a miss checks before inserting. Prototype in Rust: `HashMap<&str, Stats>` looked up by `&[u8]` (hashbrown `raw_entry`/`Equivalent`, or a `Borrow<[u8]>` key wrapper).
3. **Interning in the grammar.** `NAME` as `intern(until(…))` (winnow ADR 25 D4): the check on a miss inside the interner, the accumulator a `Vec` by `Symbol::index()`, the map gone. Measures what the slot table also saves against the hash map (#420's chain).
4. **The whole-file check, fused into the pieces** (ADR-016 §4's original idea): each `par_fold` piece checks its own range on the thread that parses it, cache-hot. Counts the same instructions as today; its point is the clock and the memory traffic, so this one is the exception where a timed run is reported beside the counts and explicitly marked as such, or it is dropped.
5. **Upper bound:** no check at all (unsound, measuring only), to say what any shape can at most win.

## What a decision would need

* **A type for text not yet checked**, if shape 2 wins. Something like a view that is bytes until a map lookup or an explicit `.text()` checks it. This is a language question (Part I 2.6): what it is called, what it can do without being checked (compare, hash, be a map key), and where the check happens. Prepare options with how others do it (Rust `&[u8]` + `from_utf8`, Go `[]byte` vs `string`, Python `bytes`/`str`, Swift `String.UTF8View`), and the cost to programs that never need it.
* **`fs::map` as `Bytes`** (a mapping without the check), needed by 1-3: a new function, or `fs::map` handing back something both a grammar and text use can take, with the check deferred to text use. Today's `Mapped` derefs to `str`, so a lazy check could not report an error there.
* **The error a program sees** for a bad byte moves from `IoError::NotText` at `fs::map` to `ParseError` at its offset (ADR-366 D3). A program that handles `NotText` would change; check `examples/` and the tests.

## To do

1. Measure 5 and 1, then 2, 3, 4. Results as one table in this issue.
2. If nothing beats today by a clear margin: close with the table, ADR-016 §4 records *measured, not worth it*.
3. Otherwise a decision basis for the owner (CLAUDE.md, *Decision rounds*): the winning shape, the type question if it needs one, `fs::map`'s form, the error change; then ADR, specification and a *To build* list here.

Depends on: winnow-grammar#24 (byte input in the backend) for 1-3 through the compiler; hand-written Rust prototypes do not need to wait. Related: #422, #420, #434, winnow-grammar#25.

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-10-18](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/664#issuecomment-6256333200)

**Measured (2026-10-18): 1BRC as a byte grammar costs more than as text today.**

`examples/1brc.nika` was changed from `fs::map` to `fs::read`, so the grammar runs as `MeasurementsOverBytes` / `parse_bytes_pieces` (ADR-366). Same output. Counted with callgrind `--branch-sim=yes` over 1 M rows, after the hashbrown switch:

| | instructions a row | mispredictions a row |
|---|---:|---:|
| as text over `fs::map` | 273.4 | 1.58 |
| as bytes over `fs::read` | 456.6 | 4.68 |

Where the bytes version pays:
- **The UTF-8 check per name, 115.6 a row and 2.67 mispredictions.** It replaces a whole-file check that cost 10.3. The ADR-366 D2 check calls `is_ascii`, and when a name is not ASCII, as many station names are, it falls to `core::str::from_utf8` instead of simdutf8.
- **The digits, 42.5 a row**, through `ascii_run` and `str::parse`.
- **The grammar runtime, 99.3 a row.**

So the bytes path pays only once what ADR-366 §4 defers is built: a mapping as `Bytes`, and text not yet checked that a map lookup checks only on a miss. The check per name should at least go through simdutf8. This issue keeps that work.

Separately, the text path is being sped up in winnow-grammar. Hand variants of three changes counted 273.4 → 232.2 a row, with mispredictions 1.58 → 1.09:
- cuts without boundary checks at positions next to an ASCII byte;
- one static searcher per scan site;
- fused runs of fixed-shape elements.

# Issue #668: std has no HTTP/HTTPS client: `std::net::connect` is blocking plain TCP

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/668).

`decision` · opened 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-18 · 0 comments

A Nikaia program cannot fetch a URL. `std::net` offers `bind`/`accept` and a blocking `connect(address)` over plain TCP (`crates/nikaia-std/src/net.rs`); `std::http1` only parses request heads for a server (`examples/http`). There is no TLS and no client.

Writing `scripts/site-issues.py` (reads the GitHub API) as a Nikaia tool, as CLAUDE.md asks of new helper tools ("Helper tools are written in Nikaia"). A prototype only works if the JSON is fetched outside (`gh api`, `curl`).

## Question for the owner

Does the language offer an HTTP(S) client in `std`? Most languages count it as basic (Python `urllib`, Go `net/http`, Rust has none in std). Decide from what the language is for, not from this one script. If yes: TLS inside `std` or through a foreign library, blocking or async, redirects, timeouts, headers.

1. ADR + specification text for the client's surface.
2. `std::http` client: `get(url; headers)` returning status, headers, body.
3. TLS (decision: own or foreign).
4. A test against a local `std::net` listener.

# Issue #673: std::regex: RE2 dialect; typed by its engine; a known pattern compiled while building and run by std's code specialised for it; run-time patterns on regex-automata

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/673).

`ready` · opened 2026-10-18 · updated 2026-10-28 · 0 comments

## What is missing

There was no `regex` in `std`. Text work used `starts_with`, `split` or counting loops; a `grammar` cannot stand in, because it is a PEG (ordered choice, possessive repetition: `a*a` never matches as a rule, and does as a regular expression).

## History

* Filed from the move of `scripts/site-issues.py` to Nikaia: fence and heading detection became a longer counting loop.
* 2026-10-26, while converting the Python scripts to Nikaia (about 45 `re.*` uses): the owner chose the RE2 dialect, a wrapper around Rust crates where possible, and `comptime RE = regex::compile("...")`.
* Checked in `regex-automata` 0.4.18's source: dense and sparse DFAs serialize and are used from a borrowed `&[u32]` without a copy (`from_bytes` validates, `from_bytes_unchecked` reads only the header: label, byte order, version, alignment); the Thompson NFA, Pike VM, one-pass DFA, lazy DFA and `meta::Regex` do not serialize; the one-pass DFA searches anchored only; `meta::Regex` builds a full DFA only up to 30 NFA states / 40 KiB.
* 2026-10-27/28, owner: tables read in place (the unchecked DFA); engines of our own where knowing the pattern pays; a known pattern is source, compiled like a `grammar`; the pattern decides what is built (`(?:…)` exists); the representation belongs in the type (`Regex[E]`, `regex::Any` for a mix); code per pattern written in `std` on a general mechanism rather than a compiler special case (#906, ADR-specialization-1); an external review added: the engine never changes the match (locate unanchored, extract groups anchored), tables written for the target's byte order. The record went through ADR-382 and ADR-384 as numbers taken elsewhere meanwhile, which led to naming records by topic (ADR-decision-records-1, #904).
* 2026-10-28, owner: start with everything on `regex::Dynamic`, add the rest step by step; leave positions out until ADR-374 (`text::Pos`) is built.
* **Built (0.0.1257, 642b0d9):** step 1 below. On the way ADR-357 D1, D2, D5 were built (a `match error` names a type by its name or path; naming every type is complete), and a keeps defect for generic `std` types was fixed. Found and filed: #917, #918, #919; the short form `catch { Type => … }` decided as ADR-catch-1 (#912).

## Decision

[ADR-regex-1](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-regex-1.md) (why, rejected alternatives), [ADR-specialization-1](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-specialization-1.md) (the mechanism S1/S2 are written on); specification Part I 2.6. In short:

* **D1-D2:** RE2 dialect, linear time, leftmost-first; `"\\d"`.
* **D3:** `regex::Regex[E]`, `E` an engine type (`Literal`, `OnePass`, `Dfa`, `TaggedDfa`, `BitNfa`, `FlatNfa`, `Dynamic`); `regex::Any` for a mix; `regex::compile(comptime p)` chooses the engine while building (a written type is a contract), `regex::dynamic(p)` compiles at run time.
* **D4:** a known pattern is source: parsed and checked while building (`NK1244`), engine and tables laid down; `std`'s calls take `comptime? self` and are emitted per known pattern.
* **D5:** the specification defines the matches, the crate is the oracle; every engine that accepts a pattern is tested; linear; nothing at run time the build could do; at least as fast as the crate; the pattern decides what is built.
* **D6:** S0 `Literal`, S1 `OnePass`, S2 `Dfa` (code under the unroll limit, table above it), S3 `TaggedDfa`, S4 `BitNfa`, S5 `FlatNfa`; the floor is `Dynamic`. A match is located unanchored (S0, S2 forward and reverse, S5) and its groups extracted anchored over the span (S1, S3, S5).
* **D7:** tables as aligned `ref Array[u32]` in the target's byte order, read in place; the crate's DFA via `from_bytes_unchecked` in a crate under `crates/unsafe`.
* **D8:** run-time patterns on `regex-automata`'s `meta::Regex`. **D9:** `--comptime` reports. **D10:** the crates parse, translate and determinise; the code that runs for a known pattern is ours.

## To build

1. ~~**Run-time patterns.**~~ Built (0.0.1257): `regex::Regex[regex::Dynamic]`, `regex::Engine`, `regex::dynamic`, `is_match`, `find`, `find_all`, `captures` (`group`, `named`), `replace_all`, `split`; a match is a `text::Match` with `m.text()` only. Not yet: `regex::Any`; positions (`m.start`, `m.end`, `from:`).
2. **Positions**, when ADR-374 is built: `m.start`, `m.end` as `text::Pos`, `from:` on `find` and `captures`, groups' positions. Tests: a multibyte text, a search from the end of a previous match.
3. **`regex::compile` on the floor:** needs ADR-333 D3 (a `comptime` parameter) and ADR-specialization-1 D7 (a result type computed from it). At first it gives `Regex[regex::Dynamic]` and checks the pattern while building (`NK1244`, the engine's message). `regex::compile` with a run-time value refused, the help naming `regex::dynamic`.
4. **S2 as a table:** `regex::Dfa`, forward and reverse dense DFA laid down for the target, a `constant` entry for the type, a crate under `crates/unsafe` opening them with `from_bytes_unchecked`; the report (D9) in `--comptime`.

# Issue #677: NK2203: a lock taken inside a lock is specified as refused (Part III C.6, ADR-281) but builds today

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/677).

`ready` · opened 2026-10-19 · updated 2026-10-19 · 0 comments

## What is wrong

Part III C.6 and Part II 12.3 say that taking a lock while a lock is held is always a compile-time error (`NK2203`), written nested, reached through a chain of calls, or opened as a scope inside the block. The compiler does not refuse it. The roadmap row for ADR-281 says the same (`NK2201` and `NK2203` "are not written"), and the `touches_a_lock` column is inferred but read by nothing (`crates/nikaia/tests/lock_column.rs`).

Found while checking the examples for the website's "What Nikaia checks" section: the page had claimed `NK2203` works, and it does not.

## Probe

Built from `develop` at `ccf982f`, `target/release/nikaia check`:

```nika
struct Account {
    balance: i64,
}

fn main() {
    let a = SharedMut(Account { balance: 100 })
    let b = SharedMut(Account { balance: 100 })
    a.update fn(mut from) {
        from.balance -= 30
        b.update fn(mut to) { to.balance += 30 }
    }
}
```

Result: `Checked`. Expected: ``error[NK2203]: `update` takes a lock, but you're already holding one here.`` (the message in Part III C.6).

The same lock twice, `a.access fn(x) { a.update fn(mut y) { y.balance += 1 } }`, is also accepted.

What is refused today: a pause inside a door (`NK2202`, `time::sleep` under `update`), and `update_all(a, b)` builds.

## To build

1. `NK2203` for a door (`access`, `update`, `set`, `access_all`, `update_all`) opened directly inside another door's block, with the message and help of C.6.
2. The same through a chain of calls, read from the `touches_a_lock` column: a call whose answer is *touches a lock* is refused, one whose answer is *undecided* is not (Part III C.4: never refuse a correct program).
3. A `task::scope` opened inside a door's block (the scope waits for its tasks).
4. Tests for each shape, the `update_all` way out accepted, and the probes above as refusals.
5. Measure the refusal against `examples/` before it lands: no program there may newly fail.
6. The website says that a hand-written nested lock is not yet refused (`index.html`, "Tasks that get stuck"); change that sentence when this lands. The commit that finishes step 6 writes `Fixes #677`.

# Issue #682: Part I does not say how integer `/` and `%` round, and does not list `div_euclid`/`rem_euclid`

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/682).

`language`, `ready` · opened 2026-10-19 · updated 2026-10-19 · 1 comment

## Where it came from

The 1BRC programs were changed to round the mean the way the official baseline does (`Math.round`, halves toward +∞; commit 02453be). In exact integer arithmetic that is `floor((2*sum + count) / (2*count))`, which needs a **floor** division when the numerator is negative. Nikaia accepts `.div_euclid(…)` on `i64`, and `tools/*.nika` already use it. The specification, however, says nothing about either point:

- **How `/` and `%` round on integers.** Today they lower to Rust's `/` and `%`, so the quotient rounds toward zero and the remainder takes the dividend's sign: `-7 / 2 == -3`, `-7 % 2 == -1`. Part I does not state this. The only place the specification mentions rounding toward zero is a float's `truncating_i32()`.
- **Which other integer divisions exist.** `div_euclid` and `rem_euclid` work, but the specification does not list them, so a program that uses them depends on behaviour nobody has decided.

What is decided already:
- ADR-285 keeps the overflow check beside the division-by-zero check.
- ADR-315 D2 makes `checked_div` and `checked_rem` return `null` on a zero divisor.

Neither decides which way the result rounds.

## What a decision has to say

1. **What `/` and `%` on integers mean.** Rounding toward zero, as in C, Rust, Java and Go, or toward −∞, as in Python. The overflow of `MIN / -1` is ADR-285's.
2. **Whether `div_euclid` and `rem_euclid`, or a floor division and modulo, are part of `std`,** under which names, and how they behave on a zero divisor and on overflow.

## Recommendation

Keep `/` and `%` as they are: rounding toward zero, with the remainder taking the dividend's sign. That is what every program written so far assumes, and what C, Rust, Java and Go readers expect. Then state it in Part I and list `div_euclid` and `rem_euclid` (always ≥ 0 for `rem`), so that a floor or "always positive" result is written explicitly and does not rely on behaviour nobody decided.

This is bookkeeping: nothing is blocked by it. The 1BRC programs use `div_euclid`, and that runs today.

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-10-19](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/682#issuecomment-6266553688)

following the recommendation : What / and % on integers mean. Rounding toward zero, as in C, Rust, Java and Go because near to hardware, make migration easier.
 div_euclid and rem_euclid are part of std

# Issue #701: std performance: `Bytes::find` is a byte loop, range indexes are not inlined, `Bytes::from(Vec)` copies

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/701).

`compiler`, `ready` · opened 2026-10-19 · updated 2026-10-19 · 1 comment

Found while writing a hand-optimised 1BRC program. Each is confirmed in the source on develop 0.0.1065.

## `Bytes::find` is a `position` loop

`crates/nikaia-std/src/bytes.rs:104`, `ByteReads for [u8]`, does `rest.iter().position(|b| *b == byte)`, and neither `find` is `#[inline]`. In the 1BRC program a row's two `find`s cost 50-78 instructions a row. The specification promises otherwise:
- ADR-320 D6: "A one-byte needle is a byte search of the kind `memchr` does".
- `std.contracts` above `[fn."Bytes::find"]`: "a byte search of the kind `memchr` does".
- ADR-296 D12: "never one byte at a time … portable word-at-a-time (SWAR) scan".

## Range indexes are not inlined

`b[i..<i + 8]` lowers to `index::at(i..i + 8)`. `impl At for Range<$t>` (`index.rs:68`, also `RangeFrom` and `RangeInclusive`) and `Span::at` (`range.rs:167`) have no `#[inline]`, while the scalar `At for $t` has `#[inline(always)]`. In the 1BRC program `Span::at` stayed a call: 10.2 instructions a row.

## `Bytes::from(Vec[u8])` copies

`bytes.rs:143-147` builds `buffer: Arc::from(bytes)` with `buffer: Arc<[u8]>`, which allocates and copies. `fs::read` followed by `Bytes::from` therefore copies the whole file twice.

## To build

1. `Bytes::find` (both impls) uses `memchr` (already a dependency through winnow) or a SWAR scan, and is `#[inline]`. Test: the existing `find` tests, plus a needle at every offset 0..64 in a 64-byte buffer.
2. `#[inline]` on the `At` impls for ranges and on `Span::at`. Check with `benches/brc/brc.sh` that nothing grows.
3. `Bytes::from(Vec[u8])` takes the allocation without a copy, e.g. a `Bytes` backed by `Arc<Vec<u8>>` or `bytes::Bytes`-style ownership. Keep `Bytes` cheap to clone and slice. Test: the pointer of the buffer is unchanged after `from`.

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-10-19](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/701#issuecomment-6277722387)

Part 3 (`Bytes::from(Vec)` without a copy) is decided and absorbed by #718: ADR-373 D2 — `Bytes(v)` takes a `Vec[u8]` over and copies nothing, and `fs::read` makes its `Bytes` that way. The commit that finishes #718 will name this issue too.

# Issue #714: Build ADR-369: a type's invariant, written as an `assert` after a struct's fields, and found where none is written

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/714).

`language`, `ready` · opened 2026-10-19 · updated 2026-10-20 · 1 comment

## History

#384 asked whether a field's bound is "an invariant of the type, or a fact within one method". ADR-306 D17 (#711) decided the second half: a field is a fact while nothing can change it.

For type invariants, the owner rejected "no case needs it" as an argument. The question was weighed by what is common:
- written invariants: Eiffel, D, Ada, Dafny;
- "check in the constructor, then rely on encapsulation": Kotlin, Java records, Rust, Go, C#;
- Nikaia's own pattern: contracts are written `assert`s (ADR-269) and loop invariants are found by the compiler (ADR-361).

The owner chose C: written and found. The `assert` goes inside the struct's body after its fields. A rule in an `impl` block is not excluded for later.

## Decision

[ADR-369](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-369.md); Part I 4.1; Part III 14.2.

```nika
pub struct Piece {
    start: i64,
    end: i64,
    assert(0 <= start && start <= end; message: "a piece ends after it starts")
}
```

**Where a rule must hold.** It holds after every construction (a literal, `with`, or the constructor's result). It holds at the end of every method that changes the value, at each `return` and `throw`. It holds after every write to a field from outside such a method. Each such point is an ADR-269 D4 claim: proved where the compiler can, checked where it cannot.

**Where a rule is a fact.** Wherever a value of the type is read, the rule is a fact over its field paths, for as long as ADR-306 D17 keeps one.

**Found rules.** For a struct with private fields that writes no rule, the compiler searches for one with ADR-361's strategies under the counted budget. A found rule is used only once it is proved. It is recorded in `nikaia.proofs`. It is never checked at runtime and never published in the ledger.

`--asserts` lists both kinds.

## To build

Depends on #711 (field paths in the walk).

1. **Parser and AST:** an `assert(...)` in a struct body after the fields; several allowed, each with `message:`. Struct-body grammar in the parser crate, which is a winnow-grammar DSL.
2. **Checker:**
   - The claim reads the struct's fields, paths from them, `comptime` values and literals, and is pure (ADR-269 D3).
   - Anything else is refused. Ask the supervisor for an NK code if a new refusal is needed.
3. **The points of D2:**
   - Generate the claim at each construction, each exit of a `mut self` method, and each outside field write.
   - Prove it, or emit the check with the rule's message, naming the point and the type.
4. **Facts of D3:** every value of the type read in a body brings its rules as facts over its paths. This covers parameters at entry, bindings after construction, fields, elements, and `self` at a method's entry.
5. **Ledger:** a written rule of a `pub` struct is published as part of the type's contract (ADR-269 D18). Changing it in the breaking direction warns (D19).
6. **Found rules (D4)**, may be a second issue: the search over private fields, certificates in `nikaia.proofs`, used only as facts.
7. **`--asserts` (D5).**
8. **Tests:**
   - a literal that breaks the rule is refuted at build time (ADR-269 D8);
   - one that may break it is checked and fails with the message;
   - a `mut self` method that breaks it in the middle and restores it passes; one that leaves it broken is caught at its exit;
   - a `pub` field write from another package is proved or checked;
   - the rule proves an index in a function that only receives a `Piece`;
   - a found rule for a private cursor struct (`0 <= at <= c.len()`) removes a check, and after an edit that breaks it, the check returns and `--asserts` says why.
9. **Measure:** proved sites over the corpus; `cmp/phase3/fast/fast.nika` with `Piece` carrying its rule.

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-10-20](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/714#issuecomment-6298747225)

**Built so far (0.0.1155–0.0.1158):** D1–D3, and three holes closed. Each hole was shown with a probe that read past the end under `remove-bounds-checks:on`.

Commits:
- f7b1900 and e664819: the type's rule is checked at each literal, at each exit of a method that changes the value, and before `self` is handed on. It is a fact at each entry. `NK1288` refuses a rule that is not a pure claim over the fields.
- 98a8e39: a type with a method that changes `self` and `throws` gets no entry fact. A failing call left the method with the rule broken, and the caller could catch the error and go on.
- b9c5cef: a type whose fields or literals another file of the package touches gets no entry fact.
- 5b7643a:
  - an *open* type gets no entry fact: one whose rule reads a `pub` field, or a `pub` type whose fields are all `pub` or defaulted. A dependency is lowered without its consumers in view, and the consumer had popped a slot;
  - a literal of the type built in another file of the package is checked against the rule.
- 531a940 and 425502a: a generic struct's rule is refused as generic, and a failure now names the type ("the rule of `T`: …").

**Still to build:**
1. **Consumer-side checks of a dependency type's rule (D2):** the rules go into the dependency's ledger, and a consumer checks them where it writes a `pub` field or builds a literal. With that, open types could keep their facts.
2. **Throwing methods:** they could keep their facts if the rule were checked at each call that may fail. That needs the pass to know which calls fail.
3. **D4** (rules the compiler finds) and **D5** (`--asserts`). #772 builds `--asserts` for `assert` and `assume` if it is not here first.
4. **A method's exit check** (`self.slots.len() == N`) is not proved yet. Writes to an element should leave `.len()` unchanged; together with #767 that gives `fast.nika`'s table index.

# Issue #717: Parallel folding without a grammar: task::cores(), Par::fold, Bytes::par_pieces, pieces claimed while running, order: (ADR-372)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/717).

`ready` · opened 2026-10-19 · updated 2026-10-20 · 5 comments

## How the question came up

The 1BRC comparative study (phase 3) wrote a hand-tuned `fast.nika` that scans bytes itself. Without a grammar, its only way onto all cores was static pieces: cut `PIECES = 8` ranges at line starts, `pieces.par_iter().map fn(p) { scan(b, p) }.collect()`, merge the list. Measured (callgrind): one table per piece, made and cleared each time - the memset alone costs 2.6 instructions/row at 8 pieces and 19.5 at 16 pieces of 32 768 slots. The hand-tuned Rust programs instead keep one table per thread and claim 1 MiB chunks with an atomic `fetch_add`. Nikaia had no core count, no `Par::fold`, and `par_fold` (Part II 10.7) exists only inside a grammar and cuts one piece per core before the work starts (ADR-296 D11).

## What was checked

* `crates/nikaia-std/src/par.rs`: `Par` has `map`, `filter`, `for_each`, `collect`, `count`, … but no `fold`.
* No `available_parallelism` in `std`; ADR-296 D11 names a `cpu::count()` that was never built.
* winnow-grammar `src/rt.rs` `fold_pieces`: `Parallelism::Auto` = `available_parallelism()` pieces (not the `user-pool` size), cut before the work, run on rayon's global pool, merged first piece first.
* Part I 5.1: options after `;` are named with a value - a bare `unordered` is not a form the language has.

## Decision (owner, decision round of 2026-10-19)

[ADR-372](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-372.md); specification Part II 10.7 and 12.6.

* `task::cores() -> i64`: the user pool's size (`user-pool`, `0` = the threads the process may run on, affinity and quota counted); `1` at `user_parallelism = no`.
* `xs.par_iter().fold(init, step, merge)`: `init` a type or `fn { … }` called once per accumulator; nothing shared.
* `b.par_pieces(sep)`: a `Par[Bytes]` of pieces ending just after `sep`.
* Pieces are claimed while the work runs, for `par_fold` too.
* `order: par::Order` - `Kept` (default: contiguous runs, merged in input order; associativity only) or `Any` (one accumulator per worker; the program promises order does not matter).
* `workers:` (default `task::cores()`) and `piece:` tune, change no result; below `1` panics naming the option.
* At `user_parallelism = no` each is one sequential fold.
* A `par_fold` failure is reported at the smallest position under either order.

## To build

1. **`task::cores()`** in `crates/nikaia-std/src/task.rs` (+ ledger entry): the user pool's thread count at `yes`, `1` at `no`. Test: a program printing `task::cores()` gives `1` at `user_parallelism = no` and `N` with `user-pool = N` in `nikaia-runtime.toml`.
2. **`par::Order`** (`Kept | Any`) in `std::par`, and **`Par::fold(init, step, merge; order:, workers:)`** in `par.rs`. `Kept`: rayon `fold` + ordered `reduce` (contiguous runs, input order). `Any`: one accumulator per worker thread (e.g. `rayon::broadcast`/per-thread slot), pieces claimed through an atomic index, merged as workers finish. Checker: `init`/`step`/`merge` asked as `par_iter` lambdas (`NK2209`, `NK2107`); `init` accepts a type name or `fn { … }`. Tests: sum over `0..1_000_000` equals the sequential sum at both orders and both `user_parallelism` values; a fold collecting into a list keeps input order under `Kept`; empty input returns `init`'s value; `workers: 0` panics naming `workers`.
3. **`piece:`** option on `par_iter` (rayon `with_min_len`/`with_max_len` around it). Test: `piece: 1` and `piece: 1_000_000` give the same result.
4. **`Bytes::par_pieces(sep: u8; piece:)`**: pieces of about `piece` bytes (runtime default, ~1 MiB), each extended to just after the next `sep`; every byte in exactly one piece, none empty. Tests: concatenation of the pieces equals `b` for inputs with/without a trailing `sep`, with no `sep` at all, and with `piece: 1`; `b.par_pieces(b'\n').fold(…)` counting lines equals `b.count(b'\n')` (+1 for an unterminated last line).
5. **`par_fold` claims pieces while it runs** (winnow-grammar `fold_pieces`, Nikaia's lowering): pieces of `piece:` bytes claimed dynamically with the existing seam repair; `order:` and `workers:` passed through; run on Nikaia's user pool, sized by `task::cores()`, not `available_parallelism()`. `Kept`: per-run accumulators merged in input order. `Any`: one per worker. Tests: existing `par_fold` tests unchanged at both orders; error position equals the sequential parse's when two pieces fail (D8); `piece: 64` on a multi-MiB input gives the sequential result.
6. **1BRC**: rewrite `fast.nika` with `b.par_pieces(b'\n').fold(Table, …, Table::merge; order: par::Order::Any)`; re-measure (callgrind counts plus perf task-clock at 1/16 codegen units) against the static-pieces version and record the comparison here. This is the measurement still owed for D4/D5 (*Kept* vs *Any* on a costly accumulator).

Not decided here (ADR-372 §5): pieces of `String` at a `char`, NUMA/heterogeneous scheduling, the default piece size (a measurement's). A public atomic `fetch_add` on `SharedMut` was not taken up.

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-10-20](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/717#issuecomment-6293778488)

Steps 1–3 are built in 137c6b0 (version 0.0.1141). `task::cores()`, `par::Order`, `Par::fold(init, step, merge; order:, workers:)` and `par_iter(piece:)` are in, with tests in `crates/nikaia/tests/parallel_folds.rs`.

- `Kept` is rayon's `fold` followed by an ordered `reduce_with`. `Any` keeps one accumulator per pool thread.
- `workers:` and `piece:` below 1 stop the program at both `user_parallelism` values.
- A walk made from a `Par` is itself a `Par`, so `fold` can follow `map` and `filter`.

**Still open:**
- **For the owner:** ADR-372 D2 says `step` *returns* the accumulator. Its own example, `fn(acc, r) { acc.record(r) }` with `Summary::merge`, and the grammar's `par_fold` both change the accumulator in place and return nothing. What is built follows the text, so the example does not compile. Which form is meant is put to the owner.
- Two defects found on the way: #757 (a named function where std takes `fn(A, A) -> A`) and #758 (a lambda's result type from `return`).
- Steps 4–6 come next: `Bytes::par_pieces`, `par_fold` claiming pieces as it runs (winnow-grammar), and 1BRC.

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-10-20](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/717#issuecomment-6293877135)

**Decided (0.0.1142): `step` and `merge` may each return the accumulator or change it in place; their result type says which.**

How it came up: ADR-372 D2 said that `step` returns the accumulator, and steps 1–3 were built that way. The ADR's own example, Part II's `par_fold`, and `examples/1brc.nika` (`fn record(ref mut self, m: Reading)`, `fn merge(ref mut self, other: Summary)`) change the accumulator in place instead. The owner chose to allow both forms.

- ADR: [ADR-372 D9](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-372.md) gives the reasons and the rejected options (returning only, in place only, `fold`/`fold_mut`).
- Spec: Part II 12.6, the `fold` paragraph.
- The rule:
  - `step: fn(A, T) -> A` or `fn(ref mut A, T)`.
  - `merge: fn(A, A) -> A` or `fn(ref mut A, A)`; in the in-place form the second argument may be taken by value or as `ref`.
  - A lambda whose body returns nothing has the in-place form.
  - `step` and `merge` choose their form independently.
  - Any other result type is `NK1102`.

# Issue #727: Lowering a package does the same work three to five times: a tenth of today's cost

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/727).

`ready` · opened 2026-10-19 · updated 2026-10-20 · 1 comment

## How it came up

CI's slowest tests (`sysroot` 94 s, `language` 87 s, `map_trust` 71 s) all lower the tools package (`crates/nikaia-std/src/tools`, 209 files, 94,500 lines, 3.5 MB of Rust). A cold `nikaia lower-std` (`NIKAIA_CACHE_DIR` empty, `NIKAIA_LOWER_THREADS=1`) takes **58.6 s of CPU**, about 1,600 lines a second; a front end usually checks 50-200 k lines a second.

## Where the time goes

`perf record --call-graph dwarf` of a cold `lower-std` at d4f932d, 8,570 samples. The figures are shares of all samples, inclusive.

**A. The same analysis runs several times (about 45 %)**

| Analysis | Runs | Total | Once would cost |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `check::walked` (the whole checker): ledger inference (`check_for_the_ledger`), the file's check, and again in the emitter (`Emitter::with_contracts` -> `check::propagation`) | 3x | 50 % | 17 % |
| `contracts::keep::buffer_plans` (in `walked` three times, in `keep::infer`, and in `with_contracts`) | 5x | 21 % | 4 % |
| `nonnegative_locals` / `nn_every` (`bounds::proven` and `Emitter::function_body`) | 2x | 12 % | 6 % |
| `Ledger::clone` in `emit_std_items_against_at`, once per file | 209x | 3 % | 0 |

**B. Method lookups scan every function of the ledger (about 24 %, mostly inside A).** For each method call these functions walk `ledger.functions` (about 5,000 keys) with `key.ends_with("::name")`, which is where `memcmp` (21 % of all samples) comes from:

| Function | Share (memcmp + self) |
| :--- | ---: |
| `keeping_method_key` (`keep.nika`) | 10.4 % |
| `owned_by_every_method` (`buffers.nika`) | 7.5 % |
| `ledger_candidates` (`check_values.nika`) | 4.3 % |
| `candidate_keys` / `keeps_at_in` (`keeps.nika`) | 1.8 % |

d4f932d already did this for `view_changes.rs`: -1 s.

**C. Clones.** `Ty::clone` takes 5.7 %, mostly in `cleanup_within` and `collect_copies`. `FnContract::clone` takes 3 %. malloc and free take about 12 % in all.

**D. `InternerContext::resolve` takes 4.5 %:** a `DashMap` with a lock, read by every check.

## Goal

A cold lower of the tools package in **a tenth** of 58.6 s of CPU, with byte-identical `package.rs`.

## To build

1. **The benchmark.** Add `benches/lowering/` (in Nikaia or as a `lower.sh` modelled on `benches/brc/brc.sh`). It does a cold lower of `crates/rs2nika/convert` (5,000 lines; callgrind instruction count) and of the tools package. It checks that the output is byte-identical to the committed one and prints a table: instructions, plus the `NIKAIA_LOWER_TIMES` phases for orientation. Count, never time (CLAUDE.md). This VM has no hardware counters, so callgrind is the count.
2. **Run each analysis once.** The checker's result for a unit is computed once and reused by the file's check and by `Emitter::with_contracts`. First establish whether the ledger pass's check sees the final ledger. If it does not, re-check only the units whose callees' contracts changed, and say so in the commit. Store `buffer_plans` and `nonnegative_locals` once per function. Share the ledger instead of cloning it per file. Test: `sysroot` (package byte-identical, one thread equals every core) plus the touched tests.
3. **Method index.** Build one map from a method's name (the key's last `::` segment) to its ledger keys, once per ledger, so the lookups never go stale. Use it in the four functions of B (and in `described_key`).
4. **Interner reads without a lock** while checking: a frozen snapshot, or `RodeoReader`.
5. **Clones on the hot paths** (`cleanup_within`, `collect_copies`, `FnContract` in BTreeMap clones): borrow instead of clone, guided by a new profile.
6. Profile again and repeat until the goal is reached. Record the table in `benches/lowering/README.md`.

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-10-20](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/727#issuecomment-6283802034)

State after eight agent rounds (versions 0.0.1099–0.0.1120), counted with `benches/lowering/lower.sh` (cold `nikaia lower --no-cache crates/rs2nika/convert/src/main.nika`, release, output byte-identical):

**16 410 M → 3 097 M Ir (−81 %).** The goal (a tenth, ~1 640 M) is not reached yet.

Built: method index; each analysis once (emitter reuses the check's facts, `Needs` read off items, program read once, trust join reuses the ledger pass); solver without arena/bound copies, ranked sorts, repeat questions answered from the book; line/column by binary search; ledger pass skips report-only walks; keep plans reused when the library is std's; text-tiers worklist; result sources stop when unchanged; `CheckResolved.contract` as a view. Lowering defects found on the way: #733, #735 (fixed), and one checker gap filed separately.

Current profile (inclusive, 3 096 M): `check::walked` 1 111 M (ledger walk 390 M); `infer_package_noted` 735 M; `bounds::proven` 577 M; parse 467 M; `keep::buffer_plans` 217 M (twice, different ledgers). malloc/free ~27 % of self.

What is left is no longer local, and needs a decision:
1. **Merge the ledger walk and the check walk** (both walk the same file with different `computes` settings): an architecture change.
2. **A faster allocator** (mimalloc): a new dependency.
3. **The interner and the parser** live in the `winnow-grammar` git dependency (`InternerContext::resolve` 97 M over a DashMap; parsing ~2 500 Ir per byte).
4. **`lg_verify`** re-checks certificates the search just made (60 M): skipping it is a trust decision.

# Issue #729: u8 gets the wrapping_, saturating_, checked_ names and truncating_u8 / checked_u8 (ADR-285 D41)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/729).

`ready` · opened 2026-10-19 · updated 2026-10-20 · 1 comment

## How it came up

The 1BRC study's `fast.nika` (phase 3, `gaps/05-u8-wrapping.nika`): `b[j] - '0'` on a `u8` is a checked subtraction, and `u8` has no `wrapping_sub`, so the program wrote `(b[j] as i32) - 48` (−8.3 instructions/row). Checked on 0.0.1097: `c.wrapping_sub(48)` with `c: u8` is refused ("A number's methods are the ones `std` describes, and none of them is called `wrapping_sub`"). Part I listed the wrapping/saturating/checked names "for `i32`, `i64`, `u32` and `u64`", and the conversions had no `u8` destination; no record gave a reason, and ADR-285 D7 says "`saturating_` wherever Rust has it".

## Decision (owner, decision round 2026-10-19)

[ADR-285 D41](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-285.md): `u8` has every name the other fixed widths have — `wrapping_`, `saturating_`, `checked_` arithmetic as for `u32` (no `_neg`/`_abs`), and `truncating_u8` / `checked_u8` out of a wider integer and an `f64`. Part I 2.2 updated; ADR-315 D1, D4 updated.

## To build

1. `std.contracts` (+ the checker's number-method table, wherever `wrapping_sub` on `u32` is described): the `u8` entries for `wrapping_add/sub/mul/div/shl/shr`, `saturating_add/sub/mul/div`, `checked_add/sub/mul/div/rem`; `truncating_u8` and `checked_u8` on `i32`, `i64`, `u32`, `u64`, `f64`. Lowered to Rust's names / `as` / `u8::try_from` as for the other widths.
2. NK1215 (narrow computation under a width-dependent name) applies to the new names as to the others.
3. Tests: `let c: u8 = 55; c.wrapping_sub(48) == 7`; `(3 as u8).wrapping_sub(5) == 254`; `(250 as u8).saturating_add(10) == 255`; `(250 as u8).checked_add(10) == null`; `300.truncating_u8() == 44`; `300.checked_u8() == null`, `200.checked_u8() == 200`; `(-1.5).truncating_u8() == 0`; `u8` has no `wrapping_neg` (refused).
4. `fast.nika` in the 1BRC study can then write `b[j].wrapping_sub(b'0')`.

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-10-20](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/729#issuecomment-6289173919)

Steps 1 to 3 are built in f24f5c1 (version 0.0.1131), with two exceptions:

- `f64::checked_u8` is missing. No `f64::checked_*` conversion exists for any width, so this is now #749.
- The test `200.checked_u8() == 200` is temporarily written as `(… ?? 0) == 200` because of the lowering defect #748.

Step 4 (`fast.nika` in the 1BRC study) is still open.

# Issue #731: `S {}` for a struct whose fields all have defaults does not parse

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/731).

`decision` · opened 2026-10-20 · updated 2026-10-20 · 0 comments

Found while building #704 (0.0.1106).

Part I says a struct literal may leave out any field that has a default (ADR-331 D5, ADR-318). Taken literally, a struct whose fields all have defaults could be written `Page {}`. The parser does not read that as a struct literal: it needs at least one field, and otherwise reads `Page` followed by an empty block. Before 0.0.1106 this was silently accepted and then failed in rustc. Now it is refused as `NK1230`, a type named as a value.

The question is whether `S {}` is a struct literal. The `{}` can also be a block, in the same places where Rust restricts struct literals, such as the head of an `if` or a `for`. This has to be prepared with an introduction from zero before it is put to the owner:
- what ADR-331 and ADR-318 decide;
- how Rust, Swift and Kotlin handle it;
- the parser's head positions;
- any alternative spelling, such as `Page()` or `Page.default()`.

**The 1BRC study.** Gap 03 of the 1BRC study: a hand-written row loop over a mapped file carries its position from one turn to the next, and the cut is refused.

```nika
let mut k = 0
while k < t.len() {
    let e = t.find("\n"; from: k) ?? return
    let row = t[k..<e]            // NK1214: `k` came through the loop
    k = e + "\n".len()
}
```

The form the help offers, `t.bytes[k..<e].text()`, checks every row as UTF-8 again, about 130 instructions a row, and the program must handle a `NotText` error that cannot happen.

**Probes on 0.0.1123** (ADR-320 D5 followed where a number came from):

| Case | Result | Correct? |
|---|---|---|
| a `mut` local carried through a loop | refused | no, too much refused |
| `e + "xy".len()` after `find("\n")` | accepted | no, too little proved |
| `e - "x".len()` | accepted | no, too little proved |
| `t[..<at - 1]` | refused | yes |

The cuts accepted wrongly stopped the program at run time (`byte position 3 is inside a scalar`). Every text cut is still checked at run time: `nikaia_std::index::text_cut` tests both ends with `is_char_boundary`. So there is no memory or UTF-8 hole, but the static rule proved less than its wording claims.

## Decision round (owner, October 20, 2026)

The owner's direction, in order:

1. A position should be a type that knows its text, lowered to a plain integer.
2. Brackets on a text invite arithmetic, so cut with methods instead.
3. Group the operations so a programmer can hold them in mind: the text, a position, a view.

**Survey of the repository:**

- **Text cuts:**
  - 38 in `crates/nikaia-std/src/tools/*.nika`, all expressible with no change of meaning:
    - 20 before or after a match;
    - 16 after a match's end: the added literal or number always equals the needle;
    - 2 at the smallest of three finds.
  - 6 in `tests/language`: `indexing.nika` tests the mismatched-literal rule, and `sequence_shapes.nika:110` cuts at a literal's length.
  - 2 in Part I.
  - None in `examples/`, `benches/` or `guide/`.
- **`find` results:** none is printed or kept in a field. One is compared with byte numbers from a table (`comptime_driver.nika:144`).
- **Grammars:** `here` and `span(p)` hand out `u32` byte offsets.

**Decision:** [ADR-374](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-374.md) replaces ADR-320 D5 and changes D6.

- `text::Pos` is a boundary in exactly one text. It takes no arithmetic and is never made from a number.
- `find` and `rfind` give a `text::Match` with `start`, `end` and `text()`.
- A text is cut with `before`, `after`, `between` and `split_at(Pos)`. There is no `[…]` on text.
- A position moves with `forward`/`back(scalars:|graphemes:|bytes: n) -> Pos?`.
- The compiler tracks which text a position belongs to with the machinery it uses for a view's sources. A position of another text, or of a text chosen at run time, is `NK1214`.
- A position cannot be a field (`NK1284`). `text::Cursor` holds a text and a position (`at`, `go`, `until`, `rest`, `text`).
- A grammar over text hands out `Pos` and `Match`.
- A cut at proven positions is not checked at run time.

Spec: Part I 2.6, Part II's grammar table, Part III (`NK1214` reworded, `NK1284`, `NK1285`).

**When to build (owner, 2026-10-27):** the architect decides, by what moves self-hosting forward (#125). It may come after more of the compiler has moved, so the moved code is migrated once. This replaces the earlier "do not start building before the owner says so".

## To build

1. **Types:**
   - `text::Pos`, a byte offset below the language, and `text::Match` in `std`.
   - `s.start()` and `s.end()`.
   - `find(needle; from: Pos) -> Match?` and `rfind -> Match?` on text. `Bytes.find` stays `i64?`.
   - Contracts in `std.contracts`.
2. **Cuts:**
   - `before`, `after`, `between` and `split_at(Pos)` lower to `&s[a..b]` with no check (D8).
   - `between` with `q < p` stops the program.
   - Remove text `[…]`: a bracket on a text becomes `NK1214`, and the help names `before`/`after`/`between`.
3. **Moves:**
   - `forward` and `back` with exactly one of `scalars:`, `graphemes:`, `bytes:`; otherwise `NK1285`.
   - `bytes:` returns `null` inside a scalar and past either end.
4. **Tracking a position's text:**
   - Give a `Pos` sources, as a view has (Part I 6.6), across parameters, results and branches.
   - Refuse a cut, move or search with a position of another text, or of `ref(a | b)` (`NK1214`).
   - Refuse a field of type `Pos` (`NK1284`).
   - Replace the number-trail analysis in `check_core_places.nika` (`check_core_places_text_cut`, `check_core_places_text_position`).
5. **`text::Cursor`:** `Cursor(t)`, `at()`, `go(p)`, `until(needle) -> ref String?`, `rest()`, `text()`.
6. **Grammars over text:** `here` gives a `text::Pos` and `span(p)` a `text::Match`.
7. **Migrate:**
   - the 38 cuts and every `find` in `tools/*.nika`; `comptime_driver.nika:144` uses `rust.before(p).bytes.len()`;
   - `benches/brc/naive.nika` (`split_at`);
   - `tests/language/indexing.nika` and `sequence_shapes.nika`, rewritten to `forward`;
   - run `lower-std`.
8. **Tests:**
   - the loop with a `mut` position is accepted;
   - `m.end.forward(scalars: 4)` on `"abcdefg"` gives `abcdef`;
   - `forward(bytes: 1)` inside `ä` gives `null`;
   - a position of `a` used on `b` → `NK1214`;
   - `ref(a | b)` → `NK1214`;
   - a number in `before` → `NK1214`;
   - `t[..]` → `NK1214`;
   - a `Pos` field → `NK1284`;
   - `forward()` and `forward(scalars: 1, bytes: 1)` → `NK1285`;
   - a cut at proven positions emits no boundary check (look at the lowering);
   - `Cursor.until` over three rows.
9. **Measure:** the 1BRC row loop as a cut by `Pos` against `t.bytes[k..<e].text()`, counting instructions with callgrind.

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-10-27](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/743#issuecomment-6440311189)

**Owner's direction, 2026-10-27.** This replaces "do not start building before the owner says so."

The architect decides when #743 is built and where it goes in the score (`docs/priorities.md`). The measure is what moves self-hosting forward (#125), not a release by the owner.

The spec (Part I 2.6) already describes `text::Match?` while `std`'s `find` gives an `i64?`. This gap stays until #743 is built. Lane G of #877 met it (`s.before(m.start)` is NK1171).
